name: Arq Premium
tagline: Encrypted backup app bundled with cloud storage and retention

pricing.notes: Working normalization from the official public pricing structure. Recheck the source page immediately before publication.

tiers.name: Arq 7
tiers.limits: License for 1 computer; back up to storage accounts you provide
tiers.notes: $49.99 one-time license, scheduled to rise to $59.99 on 2026-09-01; cloud storage is not included.

tiers.name: Arq Premium
tiers.limits: Up to 5 computers; 1 TB included cloud storage; versioned encrypted backups

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier; trial available, but the official pricing page did not expose a numeric duration
pricing.billingTerms: Arq 7 is a one-time purchase; Arq Premium is annual only; no monthly subscription
pricing.hiddenCosts: Arq 7 requires separately paid storage; Arq Premium charges $0.00599/GB/month above 1 TB, and both published prices are scheduled to increase on 2026-09-01

verdictSummary: Do not mistake the interface for the product. Arq Premium's durable value is security, infrastructure, trust, which a solo one-shot build cannot reproduce responsibly. The prompt therefore builds only the closest honest personal consolation tool.
coreLoopDIY: Build a local diagnostic or backup companion for managed backup; do not claim to replace audited security, identity, VPN, or cloud-storage infrastructure.
diyTimeEstimate: not a true replacement; consolation build in one to two days
replacementScope: consolation build only; the paid product's moat remains
requirements: Explicit README warning that this is a consolation build, not a production replacement
whatYouLose: global network or redundant storage infrastructure
whyPeopleStillPay: Arq Premium: Security subscriptions buy professional operations, audits, response capacity, redundancy, and accountability when something goes wrong.
ongoingBurden: Own threat modelling, key management, patching, backups, restore tests, incident response, privacy requests, and dependency security.

notes: Credibility row: Arq Premium survives for a structural reason, not because its interface is difficult to copy.
prompt:
Build the closest honest consolation tool inspired by Arq Premium; do not claim to replace its structural moat.
Use exactly this stack: Go 1.24 + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a local diagnostic or backup companion for managed backup; do not claim to replace audited security, identity, VPN, or cloud-storage infrastructure.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: audited cryptography and incident response; global network or redundant storage infrastructure; identity, credit, or broker-removal operations.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
